title: NestJS 12: ESM Packages, Standard Schema Validation and Native Observability
gist: NestJS 12 moves core packages to ESM, adds Standard Schema validation, rebuilds the CLI and ships @nestjs/observe, a framework-native observability SDK. Early reviewers find ESM brings tooling cleanup rather than performance gains, and APM vendors warn of framework-level lock-in.

insights.claim: NestJS 12 ships its core packages as ESM while CommonJS apps continue to work via Node.js require(esm), so it requires Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Low-friction ESM adoption lowers upgrade risk but forces Node version floors.
insights.quote: Core packages now ship as ESM, but CommonJS applications keep working through Node.js require(esm) support
insights.locator: The ESM change is the headline

insights.claim: Preview benchmarks found no meaningful startup or memory gains from ESM, so it is a tooling and configuration cleanup rather than a performance upgrade.
insights.speaker: Anton Chapala
insights.so_what: Teams should not expect runtime performance benefits to justify migration effort.
insights.quote: is a massive cleanup of tooling and configuration debt
insights.locator: The ESM change is the headline

insights.claim: New ESM projects default to Vitest and oxlint and Rspack replaces webpack as the monorepo bundler, while nest upgrade moves packages to v12 and TypeScript 6 but deliberately does not convert projects to ESM, Vitest or oxlint.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Defaults track the shift away from webpack and legacy toolchains to Rust/Go-based tooling.
insights.quote: It deliberately does not convert projects to ESM, Vitest or oxlint.

insights.claim: Early adopters report friction: AWS Lambda runtimes need --experimental-require-module, path aliases break under ESM and Fastify middleware exceptions can hang.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: ESM migration pitfalls remain in serverless and aliasing setups.

insights.claim: Follow-up v12.1 added built-in cookies, CSRF protection and security headers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Rapid follow-ups show the framework absorbing middleware concerns into core.

insights.claim: Route decorators accept a schema option for any Standard Schema compatible object, so Zod, Valibot and ArkType work without third-party wrappers, while class-validator remains the documented default.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Standard Schema reduces validator lock-in across the TypeScript ecosystem.
insights.quote: accept a schema option taking any Standard Schema compatible object

insights.claim: Building on a spec instead of directly on Zod keeps validator choice in developer hands, though types still need manual annotation because Nest relies on legacy TypeScript decorators.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Legacy decorators limit the type-inference benefits of schema-first validation.
insights.quote: keeps the choice in my hands while removing the boilerplate

insights.claim: @nestjs/observe hooks into Nest's lifecycle via an instrument option rather than patching the HTTP server, reporting traces in terms of controllers and providers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Framework-native tracing yields richer context than generic HTTP instrumentation.

insights.claim: Scout Monitoring warns the observability SDK is NestJS-only, lacks cross-stack correlation out of the box and risks vendor lock-in at the framework level.
insights.speaker: Scout Monitoring
insights.so_what: First-party observability competes with APM vendors and OpenTelemetry-style neutrality.
insights.quote: vendor lock-in at the framework level

insights.claim: A new nest deploy command forwarding to the Mau platform points toward first-party services around the framework.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Open-source frameworks are moving to monetize through hosted platforms and tooling.
insights.quote: points the same way towards first-party services
